title: Measuring the Moon
subtitle: Marks on a real picture, a scale from a known length, and a size in kilometers
body:
Step 1 of 8 read

A real picture of the Moon

This is a real picture: the Moon, photographed by NASA’s Galileo spacecraft on 7 December 1992 as it flew past the Earth on its way to Jupiter. It is an enhanced-color composite, shown here in gray. Enhanced means the contrast was stretched to show differences in the ground, so its gray levels are for the eye and are not a measure of the light the Moon reflects. The Observatory calls such a picture display-only: you may mark it and measure it in pixels, and nothing more.

A picture has no scale of its own. This one is 496 pixels across, and a pixel is not a kilometer. The pixels are numbered from the lower left, x to the right and y up, and the disc is cropped close: its right edge touches the last column. In this investigation you give the picture a scale and take one measurement off it.

title: Measuring the Moon
subtitle: Marks on a real picture, a scale from a known length, and a size in kilometers
body:
Step 8 of 8 read

What you worked out

A picture has no scale until you give it one, and the scale you give it is a measurement of yours, resting on a length you assumed and on two marks you placed. With it, a circle on a feature gave a size in kilometers, about 630 km for the plain, and the tool’s stated uncertainty covered only the rounding of your marks. The softness of the edge, the crop at the right and the assumed diameter are not in it. And because the picture is a display picture, its gray levels are not light: you measured where things are and how big they are, and nothing about how bright.
